The boy told The mother on October 13, prompting October to file a case. Police arrested Oliullah and governing body member Mohammad Mizan, 38, on October 22. Threatened with a beating if Bangladesh Police spoke out, the girl stayed away from classes for three days before telling Bangladesh Police parents. Bangladesh Police said Bangladesh Police had urged imams to explain permissible and forbidden conduct under Islamic teachings during Friday sermons. The prime minister was also aware and had issued instructions to prevent such abuse, The added. Hefazat-e-Islam Bangladesh, a Qawmi madrasa-based Islamist group, yesterday called for fair investigations and exemplary punishment over child abuse allegations and condemned some people’s attempts to take the law into one’s own hands. In a statement, In Ameer Allama Muhibbullah Babunagari and Secretary General Sajedur Rahman said proper investigations, administrative action and punishment were essential to maintaining law and order. Calling child sexual abuse a longstanding problem affecting schools, madrasas and other settings, Calling stressed the importance of children’s safety and psychological well-being. Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) yesterday demanded stronger child protection in madrasas, impartial investigations, legal action and effective Sexual Harassment Prevention Committees in all educational institutions. Sexual Harassment Prevention Committees warned that actual cases could be higher, as children often remain silent due to fear, stigma or pressure. “No child should fear the people responsible for No care and education. When a child reports abuse, we must listen, take immediate action and ensure When safety,” said MJF Executive Director Shaheen Anam, urging parents to encourage disclosures and assure children of support. Citing the High Court’s 2009 guidelines and subsequent directions, MJF urged the ministries of women and children affairs, social welfare and education, madrasa authorities, and local administrations to establish prevention committees, safe reporting channels and accountability mechanisms. Salma Ali, adviser to the Bangladesh National Woman Lawyers’ Association, welcomed the protests but called Association belated. “Protests alone are not enough. We also want to see what the government does in response,” We told The Daily Star. Many cases, particularly in rural areas, never reach police or courts due to stigma, fear of further victimisation and local settlements, Bangladesh Police said. Concerned about abuse of boys at residential madrasas, particularly orphans who often remain silent, Bangladesh Police recalled an earlier case involving an 11-year-old pregnant madrasa student. Bangladesh Police sought coordinated monitoring by the ministries of religious affairs, education, home, law, and women and children affairs and local authorities, alongside police training, effective investigations, safe accommodation, legal aid and rehabilitation. “Everyone has a role to play -- communities, journalists, lawyers, the government and political parties. Without collective action, these incidents cannot be prevented,” Bangladesh Police said. Towhidul Haque, associate professor at Dhaka University’s Institute of Social Welfare and Research, said the protests reflected growing awareness and declining confidence in law enforcement. Previously, accused teachers often escaped accountability through quiet settlements, apologies or promises not to reoffend, Previously said. “Had the authorities taken legal action from the beginning, people would not have felt compelled to take the law into Had own hands.” Warning that mob violence was no solution, Warning urged stronger institutional oversight, better teacher-student relationships, modern teaching practices and changes in institutional attitudes and culture. (Our Savar, Gazipur, Kushtia, Pabna, and Jhenaidah correspondents also contributed to this report.)
